text: This is just a vent or rant, I don't know, but basically, I got hired at this new company as a backend developer, and I was excited about my first remote job. The company is building its project, and I'm the only backend developer, responsible for the whole server. I like a challenge, so I went to work. Two months in, I realized there was no proper documentation system other than Google Docs, so I suggested integrating Swagger into the backend (I had to ask, since people are apparently very strict about tickets). The manager said yes, but maybe in the future (which, as I learned, means no). Three months in, my probation ended, and I asked the manager about the raise in my contract. He told me HR was making new policies, and once that was done, we'd see. By this time, I was also realizing the project was heading in a very messy direction, since the manager just wanted tickets finished and story points completed. I told the manager it wasn't right and that we really should rework it. He said there was no need, and since I couldn't do much more than argue, I went back to tickets. Seven months in, the manager brought in a fresh new design and presented it as some kind of favor to me. It turned out there was no rework; it was just another Figma design with even vaguer requirements. I got annoyed, so I told someone on the upper team. The manager said to start working on the backend according to the new design and that it's okay to have your code scrapped, completely normal (he didn't mention why the code was being scrapped, which was misunderstood requirements). The next day, he told the team to stop working on the project and wait for instructions from higher up: ""There's nothing wrong with the project; it's just being reworked according to some new requirements."" Today, the manager said the old project is okay, but we now have to make a version 2 of it from scratch, though the old project is completely fine and we can reuse things from it. I told him that just means the old project was wrong, and he said that, as he'd said, it's completely fine; we'll just be making improvements. Anyway, that's what happened today, so I was really annoyed and needed to let it out.

text: My boss called me in for a 1-on-1. I'd already had an eerie feeling for the past two weeks, since I was being assigned lame tickets and no actual project work. text: I'm about 8 weeks into a 12-week summer internship here in Texas, and I haven't done or learned as much as I'd hoped. The company is small, and the full-time employees work remotely in a different city. They come into town once a week or so to work with the interns, but most days it's just the interns in the office, with a daily video stand-up. After that, it's just Slack and the occasional call and screen-share to work something out. The full-timers are nice and really patient with me, but I just don't see much of them. The company is building out its framework right now, so requirements and expectations are constantly changing, which I feel hasn't been the best environment for me. I get really lost at times, and it can bring me to a dead stop where I have no idea what I'm supposed to be doing. I end up having to strategize with the full-timers over Slack, which... I don't know, I don't like it. I'd rather work things out in person and do pair programming; I feel like so much gets lost when you're just talking about something over Slack. Some days are great: I know my task through and through and have a good time working through it. But a lot of the time, I have no idea what I'm supposed to be doing and have to sit around trying to look busy. I feel like I was thrown into their somewhat obscure tech stack with minimal guidance. I've talked to the CEO about this several times and explained that I need some guidance and a chance to learn things (a tutorial or some training) so I can be more helpful, but their response was that they want interns doing actual work, not tutorials, and that if I need help learning something, I should just communicate with the full-timers. I'd be okay with that if they were around more often (they're actually very helpful when I get face time with them), but like I said, it's really hard for me to learn things from someone pinging me on Slack. The office is really quiet, which can get depressing at times; no one really talks, and there isn't much chemistry among the interns. I guess I just expected more mentorship and learning, and I didn't expect the office to be JUST interns 80% of the time. I feel like this company had no business hiring interns, since they don't have the infrastructure or organization to support them. At the same time, I feel guilty and upset with myself that I haven't done or learned as much as I wanted to. The days when I'm completely lost, no full-timers are in the office, and I'm stuck with the other interns are incredibly grueling and depressing. I just feel so restricted and anxious, and I'm not sure what I should do. I don't want my summer to be completely wasted, and I want to leave this job having gained something.
